summary:
Terrestrial Analog Finder is a web-based application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps users discover and compare locations on Earth that have environmental and terrain characteristics similar to selected regions of the Moon and Mars.

The system combines NASA scientific datasets, including Earth climate observations, lunar surface temperature and topography, and Martian temperature and elevation data. It analyzes these characteristics to rank potential terrestrial analog sites based on their similarity to planetary environments.

The application provides an interactive map, global heat layer, ranked candidate locations, individual site comparisons, and a comparison matrix for multiple planetary targets.

This project is important because Earth-based analog environments can support scientific research, educational activities, and the preparation of future planetary exploration missions. It transforms complex planetary data into an accessible visual tool for exploration and comparison.
details:
What it does and how it works

Before anyone sends a rover, a drill, or a crew to the Moon or Mars, they usually test their equipment and procedures somewhere on Earth that resembles the target. These places are called terrestrial analogs. The hard part is choosing one. A site can look like Mars geologically but be nothing like it in temperature or pressure, and the data needed to compare them is scattered across different sources, units, and resolutions.

Terrestrial Analog Finder puts that comparison in one interactive web app. You pick a world (the Moon or Mars) and a target such as Shackleton crater’s rim, Mare Tranquillitatis, or Jezero. Then you set what matters for your purpose by adjusting the weight of each factor: temperature, air and water, geology, terrain, sun geometry, wind and dryness, and remoteness. The app re-ranks Earth sites instantly and shows a map, a detailed side-by-side view with the original values and sources, and a clear list of what each site does not capture. It also scans a global grid of Earth locations to suggest preliminary regions worth studying beyond the known sites in our catalog.

Under the hood, a processing pipeline reads data from NASA missions (LRO Diviner and LOLA, MRO Mars Climate Sounder, MGS MOLA), cleans it, runs consistency checks, and saves a traceable snapshot. Earth climate and elevation come from NASA POWER and OpenTopoData. The score itself is a transparent weighted formula, not a black-box model, so users can always see why a site ranked where it did.

Benefits

Researchers and student teams get a shortlist of sites to investigate, instead of defaulting to the one famous analog.

Field-planning teams can discuss priorities before choosing where to work, and see which properties a site supports and which it doesn’t.

Educators get an interactive way to show that “similarity” is multi-dimensional, and that the best site changes depending on the question you ask.

Every value is labeled as observed, model-derived, reference, or editorial, so nothing is hidden behind a single number.

Intended impact

The goal is to improve the early exploration and comparison stage, helping people understand and justify their choices before spending time and money on detailed surveys. We hope it makes analog-site selection more transparent and makes planetary science more approachable for students and small teams. These are intended impacts, not proven results. We haven’t yet measured cost savings or mission-risk reduction, and the app is not a landing-safety or mission-certification tool. It supports early planning and does not replace expert review or field surveys.

Tools and technologies

TypeScript and JavaScript across the project, with React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, and Leaflet for the interactive interface and maps. The backend uses Node.js and Express with a PostgreSQL database (via Drizzle ORM), Zod for validation, and an OpenAPI contract so the frontend and server share the same data definitions. The project is organized as a pnpm monorepo, tested with Node’s built-in test runner, versioned on GitHub, and developed on Replit. Data sources include NASA POWER, LRO, MRO, MGS, Mars Climate Database, LROC Lunar Pit Atlas, USGS lunar geology, GLiM, and NASA GIBS imagery.

What makes it creative

It turns scattered planetary and environmental data into one question people actually ask: which Earth site resembles this target, and in what ways?

It makes priorities part of the result. Changing the weights changes the answer, so users help define what “similar” means.

It combines a catalog of known analog sites with a global grid for broader discovery, and links a lunar pit/crater atlas to the comparison.

It shows its reasoning and its limits: sources, value types, shared and unshared geology tags, and measurement caveats appear next to every score.

Factors we considered

We were careful about scientific honesty. Similarity is partial, so no Earth site can reproduce lunar vacuum, Martian pressure, gravity, or radiation, and the app says so. Our terrain indicator is a simple elevation-difference measure, not a slope or traversability assessment. Some inputs, such as geology tags and remoteness, are editorial estimates, and the app labels them that way. The weighting is rule-based and explainable rather than machine learning, and the global grid is a coarse exploration tool, not a local survey. We also checked consistency across data units, projections, and resolutions, and validated the build with automated tests, type checking, and a production build.
